newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Profit slides at S.Korea's Samsung on chip sales.
newsitem.headline: Profit slides at S.Korea's Samsung on chip sales.

text.p: Slumping computer chip prices drove net profit at South Korea's Samsung Electronics down 93 percent in 1996, the company said on Thursday, but analysts expect a recovery this year at the world's largest memory chip maker.

after-tax net profit slid to a provisional 164.16 billion won ($190.4 million) from 2.51 trillion won in 1995, a company official said. Turnover fell slightly to a provisional 15.87 trillion won from 16.19 trillion won.
Samsung officials said a freefall in the prices of 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips hampered profits. DRAM sales account for about 35 percent of sales.

Prices of 16-megabit DRAM chips, currently the most widely installed memory chips in personal computers, fell about 80 percent in 1996 due to global oversupply, cutting heavily into Samsung's revenue base.

But the 16-megabit DRAM chips are expected to remain the industry standard until about mid-1998 despite the development of faster 64-megabit DRAM chips, a situation which analysts expect to benefit Samsung given its large 16-megabit production.
The profit result was generally welcomed by investors, who pushed up the group's shares in an otherwise falling market. Samsung ended 100 won higher at 57,300.
"The results are well above our earlier expectations," said Ilsuk Han, an analyst at ING-Barings Securities. "I think the company's non-chip sectors boosted the bottom line."
Analysts added that a much slower decline in memory chip prices, along with swift growth in the telecommunications sector, should help propel a considerably recovery in Samsung's profits in 1997.
Unit prices of 16-megabit DRAMs recently edged up to around $9-$9.50 in international spot markets from around $6 late last year, the analysts said.
But they said the average price would remain below earlier highs, at around $8 this year, compared with $18 in 1996 and $50 in 1995.
The market was also watching the performance of the group's telecommunications and information products, which account for about 30 percent of Samsung's total sales and are seen rising.

On Thursday, Samsung said it expected sales of $4.2 billion from its telecommunications division in 1997 and announced plans to boost this year's investment in the telecommunications sector by 27 percent to $715 million.

Telecommunication products range from telephones using code-division multiple access (CDMA) technology, electronic telephone exchange systems and computer terminals to hand phones, networking systems and multimedia products.

"The telecommunications sector will be the major contributor to a recovery in the company's profits this year," said Han at ING-Baring. "A relatively small burden from depreciation costs should also help."
CDMA, the digital data transmission technology used in cellular telephones, is in commercial service in only a few areas, including South Korea, the United States and Hong Kong.
In a company statement, Samsung said it would strengthen international competitiveness by establishing alliances with leading overseas companies.
"Samsung is determined to strengthen and sustain the already positive marketing position of its CDMA terminals and systems, fibre optics and mutifunctional office machines," it said.
"Samsung Electronics predicts that mobile communications and networking will be the areas of the high growth for the 21st century, and thus has decided to pursue them aggressively," the company said.
